1121.title: The miqat, where pilgrims begin
1121.hook: pilgrims enter ihram at set points around Mecca
1121.carry: at the miqat, a traveler becomes a pilgrim
1121.howItsDone: Pilgrims enter ihram at or before the miqat on their route; some flying in change into ihram before boarding or on the plane, and airlines may announce when the miqat is near.

segments.voice: Yesterday, umrah: lesser and greater. The visit any time of year, and Hajj on its own days.

Somewhere over the desert, on the way into Jeddah, a plane full of pilgrims gets an announcement: the aircraft will soon pass the point. Up and down the aisles, people who boarded in ordinary clothes are already changed, or changing in the cramped bathrooms, or quietly saying the words that mark the start. Nothing on the ground below looks different. There's no gate, no fence, no sign you could see from the window. But the line is there, and they know it.
screen: `OVER THE DESERT.` → `THE AIRCRAFT WILL SOON PASS THE POINT.` → `NO GATE, BUT A LINE.`

segments.voice: First, what a miqat is: a set point, a boundary place, where pilgrims heading for Mecca enter ihram, the sacred state of the pilgrimage. Before it, a person is a traveler. Past it, for Hajj or umrah, they must already be a pilgrim. Second, who set them. A hadith from Ibn Abbas in Sahih al-Bukhari names the places: Dhul Hulayfah for the people of Medina; al-Juhfah for the people of Sham, the lands to the north; Qarn al-Manazil for the people of Najd; Yalamlam for the people of Yemen. Other reports add a point for the people of Iraq. And the points are for the people of those lands and for anyone else who passes through them on the way to Hajj or umrah. Whoever lives closer enters ihram from where they are, and the people of Mecca from Mecca itself. Third, why a line at all. The places sit at different distances from Mecca, out on the roads people actually traveled, so the boundary meets each traveler on their own road. Nobody walks into the sacred state by accident, and nobody slips past it unnoticed. Hence the plane announcement: scholars hold that the old points still apply in the air, so pilgrims enter ihram as they cross them, or before. Fourth, the word. Miqat also carries the sense of an appointed time. In surah seven, when Musa comes to his meeting with his Lord on the mountain, the Qur'an uses this same word for that appointed meeting. A place and a time, both set in advance, both kept. The miqat is where an ordinary journey becomes a pilgrimage.
screen: `WHERE THE TRAVELER BECOMES A PILGRIM.` · `FOUR PLACES, NAMED IN BUKHARI.` · `THE LINE MEETS YOU ON YOUR ROAD.` · `A SET PLACE, AN APPOINTED TIME.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a doorway you cross every day without noticing: your front door, the door to your work, the door of your car. Picture yourself pausing there for one breath before you step through, the way a pilgrim knows the point is coming. What would you want to leave outside, and what would you want to carry in?

1122.title: Two white cloths
1122.hook: men wear two unstitched white cloths; women wear modest ordinary clothes
1122.howItsDone: Men entering ihram for Hajj or Umrah put on two unstitched white cloths, one around the waist and one over the shoulders; women wear their own modest clothes. Pilgrims make their intention at the miqat and stay in ihram until the rites release them.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the miqat, the set boundary where an ordinary journey becomes a pilgrimage. Your line: the boundary.

Two pieces of white cloth. No seams, no buttons, no collar, no label. One wraps the waist, the other goes over the shoulders. That's the whole outfit. A pilgrim reaches yesterday's boundary, takes off the clothes that said who he was at home, the suit or the uniform or the team jersey, and puts these on. The man next to him does the same, and the man next to him. Within an hour, you can't tell the surgeon from the taxi driver. Today, the word for what has just happened to them.
screen: `NO SEAMS, NO LABEL.` → `THE CLOTHES FROM HOME COME OFF.` → `NOBODY CAN TELL WHO IS WHO.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Ihram isn't really the name of the cloth. It's a state the pilgrim enters, at the boundary, with an intention. The two cloths are how that state looks from outside, and people call them the ihram too. Second, how the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ described it. Someone asked him what a person in ihram should wear. The report is in Sahih al-Bukhari, and his answer is a surprise: he didn't describe the outfit. He listed what to leave off. No shirts, no turbans, no trousers, no hooded cloaks, no leather socks. The clothes are defined by what's missing. Whatever is cut and sewn to the shape of a body, with its fashion and its rank, stays home. Third, the women. A woman in ihram doesn't wrap herself in two white cloths. She wears her own ordinary, modest clothes, and another report in Bukhari says she doesn't wear a face veil or gloves in that state. So the rule isn't one uniform for everybody. It's simplicity for everybody, in the shape that fits. Fourth, what it does. Put a crowd from everywhere into the same plain dress, and the usual signals go quiet. Nobody's watch is on show. Nobody's accent shows in the cut of a coat. Some pilgrims say the two white cloths remind them of a shroud, plain cloth like the cloth Muslims are buried in, and that thought travels with them the whole journey. Whatever the cloth means to a given pilgrim, the effect is the same. For a few days, the person inside it is just a person, standing among people, dressed alike.
screen: `A STATE, NOT JUST A CLOTH.` · `DEFINED BY WHAT'S LEFT OFF.` · `WOMEN: THEIR OWN MODEST CLOTHES.` · `THE SIGNALS GO QUIET.`

segments.voice: Take off one thing you wear partly so people will notice it, a logo, a watch, a piece of jewelry, and set it aside. Sit for a moment and notice whether you feel any lighter, or any barer. If you pray, hold the picture of the pilgrims in their plain cloth and say a verse you know; if not, stay with the breath, being nobody in particular.
Ihram. The sacred state a pilgrim enters at the boundary, and the plain clothes that show it. Today's word.
Your line: all dressed alike. The cloth hides the rank and leaves the person. See you tomorrow.

1123.title: What ihram forbids
1123.hook: no perfume, no cutting hair, no hunting, no quarrelling
1123.howItsDone: Pilgrims in ihram avoid perfume, cutting hair and nails, hunting, marital relations and quarreling until the rites release them; the details and the remedy for a slip are set out in each school of Islamic law.

segments.voice: Yesterday: ihram, the sacred state, and the two plain cloths that show it. Your line: all dressed alike.

A pilgrim is standing at Arafah with the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ when his mount throws him. He falls and dies there, still in his two white cloths. The report is in Sahih al-Bukhari. The people around him turn to the Prophet: what now? His instructions are short. Wash him with water and lote leaves. Shroud him in his two cloths. No perfume. Don't cover his head. Then the reason: he'll be raised on the Day of Resurrection still calling out the pilgrim's cry. Even death, in this story, doesn't take him out of ihram. Today, what that state holds a person back from.
screen: `A PILGRIM FALLS AT ARAFAH.` → `NO PERFUME. HEAD UNCOVERED.` → `RAISED STILL A PILGRIM.`

segments.voice: First, the body. Once a pilgrim is in ihram, some ordinary things stop. No perfume, on the skin or the cloth. No cutting hair: the Qur'an tells pilgrims not to shave their heads until the offering has reached its place, so the haircut becomes part of the ending, not the middle. Scholars add nails to the same list. Second, the creatures. The Qur'an says plainly, in surah five, that wild game is not to be killed on the pilgrimage. A person who might hunt at home lets the animals of the sanctuary be. Third, the tongue, and this one surprises people. In surah two, Pickthall's translation reads: "there is (to be) no lewdness nor abuse nor angry conversation on the pilgrimage." You met that verse back on day three hundred fifty-four. Not just no fighting. No angry conversation. A crowd, the heat, the lines, the lost luggage, an elbow in the ribs, and the instruction is: don't argue. Of everything on the list, that one asks the most patience. Fourth, what the rules are for. Each is something small and ordinary, a scent, a trim, a sharp word. None of them is wrong at home. In ihram, they're set down for a while. The two cloths are what people see. The restraint is what they don't see, and it goes all the way down. That's why the man who fell at Arafah was left unperfumed and bareheaded. The rules weren't a costume he could take off. They were the state he was in, and he stayed in it.
screen: `NO PERFUME, NO HAIRCUT.` · `LET THE WILD GAME BE.` · `NO ANGRY CONVERSATION.` · `THE RESTRAINT GOES ALL THE WAY DOWN.`

1124.title: The talbiyah
1124.hook: here I am, O Allah, here I am, no partner have You
1124.howItsDone: Pilgrims begin reciting the talbiyah when they enter ihram and repeat it often, men aloud and women more quietly, through the days of the pilgrimage until the stoning on the day of sacrifice, according to the reports of the Prophet's Hajj.

segments.voice: Yesterday: what ihram forbids, perfume, haircuts, hunting and angry words, set down for a while. Your line: restraint is the dress.

Somebody calls your name across a room. Before you've decided anything, before you know what they want, you answer. Here. Yes? I'm here. In the Qur'an, Ibrahim is told to make a call of his own. Pickthall's translation of surah twenty-two: "And proclaim unto mankind the Pilgrimage. They will come unto thee on foot and on every lean camel; they will come from every deep ravine." A call goes out. On the roads to Mecca, people answer it, out loud, over and over. Today, the answer.
screen: `SOMEONE CALLS YOUR NAME.` → `PROCLAIM THE PILGRIMAGE.` → `THEY WILL COME.`

segments.voice: First, the words. Abdullah ibn Umar reported the talbiyah of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and it's kept in Sahih al-Bukhari. In Arabic it begins: labbayk Allahumma labbayk. In English, roughly: here I am, O Allah, here I am. Here I am, You have no partner, here I am. Praise and blessing are Yours, and the dominion. You have no partner. That's all of it, a handful of short lines said again and again. You first heard labbayk back on day two hundred eighty-four. Second, the shape of the word. Labbayk isn't a request. It's a reply, the word for answering someone who has called you: here I am, at your service. The pilgrim isn't starting a conversation, but responding to one. Some readers connect that to Ibrahim's call in surah twenty-two: he proclaimed, and pilgrims, generation after generation, are still answering. Third, the line that comes twice: no partner have You. In a journey full of crowds, rituals and holy places, the talbiyah keeps pointing past all of it, to one God alone. Fourth, the sound. A report in Tirmidhi has the Prophet saying that the angel Jibril came and told him to have his companions raise their voices with the talbiyah. So the roads, the buses, the airports and the tents carry it out loud, men's voices raised, women's usually lower. A pilgrim begins it on entering ihram and keeps it going for days. The man in yesterday's story, who died in ihram, would be raised still saying it. Here I am.
screen: `HERE I AM, O ALLAH, HERE I AM.` · `A REPLY, NOT A REQUEST.` · `NO PARTNER HAVE YOU.` · `RAISE YOUR VOICES.`

segments.voice: If you're Muslim, or pray, say labbayk Allahumma labbayk quietly and slowly a few times, and notice that each line is an answer. If not, let the English run through your mind, here I am, and notice what it would mean to answer a call before you know everything it will ask.
Talbiyah. The pilgrim's cry, labbayk, here I am, said from the moment of ihram. Today's word.

1125.title: Circling the House
1125.hook: seven circuits anticlockwise around the Ka'ba
1125.howItsDone: Pilgrims perform tawaf by walking seven circuits around the Ka'ba counterclockwise, starting and ending at the corner of the black stone, often reciting Qur'an or making du'a; men walk briskly in the first three circuits of the arrival tawaf.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the talbiyah, labbayk, the pilgrim's answer to a call. Your line: labbayk.

After miles of here I am, the pilgrims arrive. They come through the gates of the mosque in Mecca, and there it is: a plain stone building draped in black cloth, standing in the middle of a wide open floor. The Qur'an, in surah twenty-two, names what pilgrims do at this House, and Pickthall's translation puts it in a few words: "go around the ancient House." Not enter it. Not climb it. Go around it. Today, the walk that goes in circles on purpose.
screen: `THEY ARRIVE.` → `A PLAIN HOUSE IN BLACK CLOTH.` → `GO AROUND THE ANCIENT HOUSE.`

segments.voice: First, the shape. Tawaf means going around. The pilgrim circles the Ka'ba with it on the left, so the whole crowd turns the same way, counterclockwise, like one slow wheel. You met the House itself back on day forty-two. Second, the count. Jabir ibn Abdullah gave a long account of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ's pilgrimage, kept in Sahih Muslim. When the Prophet reached the House, Jabir says, he went around it, moving briskly for three circuits and walking for four. Seven in all. The brisk pace for the first three has a name: ramal. Third, what kind of act it is. A report in Tirmidhi has the Prophet saying that going around the House is like prayer, except that in it you may speak, so whoever speaks should speak only good. A prayer you can walk, and even talk in, as long as the talk is good. People recite, make their own requests, repeat words of praise, or walk in silence. Fourth, the center. Every circle needs one point that doesn't move. Crowds from everywhere, in plain cloth, all turning around the same still house. In Islam the Ka'ba is not the one worshipped; it's the House, and the worship is for God alone. But the walk teaches with the body something that's hard to teach with words. Everything in the crowd is moving. The center isn't. Each circuit brings the pilgrim back to the corner where it began, and the next one starts again from there.
screen: `THE HOUSE ON THE LEFT.` · `THREE BRISK, FOUR WALKING.` · `A PRAYER YOU CAN WALK.` · `EVERYTHING MOVES BUT THE CENTER.`

segments.voice: Walk seven slow laps of a room or a yard, always in the same direction, counting on your fingers if it helps; this isn't tawaf, just a way to feel its shape in the body. If you pray, say words of praise you know as you go; if not, keep your attention on your steps. When the seven are done, stand still and breathe.
Tawaf. Going around the Ka'ba, seven times, with the House on the left. Today's word.
Your line: around the center. Everything else can turn while the center holds. See you tomorrow.

1126.title: The black stone
1126.hook: pilgrims kiss, touch or point to it, as the Prophet ﷺ did
1126.howItsDone: During tawaf, pilgrims begin each circuit at the black stone; those who can reach it kiss or touch it, and others raise a hand toward it from a distance and say Allahu akbar.

segments.voice: Yesterday: tawaf, seven circuits around the House, with the center standing still. Your line: around the center.

Umar ibn al-Khattab walks up to a corner of the Ka'ba, bends toward a dark stone set into the wall, and kisses it. Then he straightens up and speaks to it. The words are kept in Sahih al-Bukhari, and they're blunt. I know you are a stone. You can neither harm nor help. If I had not seen the Prophet kiss you, I would not have kissed you. Today, the stone, and why a man who said all that still bent down to it.
screen: `UMAR KISSES THE STONE.` → `I KNOW YOU ARE A STONE.` → `ONLY BECAUSE THE PROPHET DID.`

segments.voice: First, where it is. The black stone is set into one corner of the Ka'ba, the corner where each circuit of yesterday's tawaf begins and ends. Second, Umar's words, and what they guard against. He says out loud what someone watching might wonder: is this stone a power? No. It can't harm and it can't help. Whatever honor it has comes from one place: the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ honored it. So the kiss isn't worship of a stone. It's following a person, in a small physical way, exactly as he did. Third, the crowds. Today, getting close enough to kiss the stone can mean a long, hard push through a packed crowd. Here another report in Bukhari helps. Ibn Abbas says the Prophet once went around the House riding a camel, and whenever he came to the corner, he pointed to it and said Allahu akbar. He didn't get down. He didn't push. He pointed. So pilgrims have three ways: kiss it if you can reach it, touch it with a hand, or, from a distance, raise a hand toward it and say God is greatest. Fourth, what that means for the crowd. In this report, the pointing isn't a fallback. It's the Prophet's own way that day. Nobody needs to shove an old man aside to honor a stone that, in Umar's words, can't help anyone. A raised hand from far back in the crowd is a full greeting. A salute to the corner, and the circuit goes on.
screen: `THE CORNER WHERE EACH CIRCUIT BEGINS.` · `IT CAN NEITHER HARM NOR HELP.` · `KISS, TOUCH, OR POINT.` · `THE RAISED HAND IS A FULL GREETING.`

1127.title: Behind Ibrahim's station
1127.hook: two units of prayer behind the station of Ibrahim (2:125)
1127.howItsDone: After completing tawaf, pilgrims pray two rak'ahs behind the station of Ibrahim if there is room, or elsewhere in the mosque when it is crowded, often reciting al-Kafirun and al-Ikhlas.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the black stone, kissed, touched, or saluted from far back in the crowd. Your line: a salute to the corner.

The seventh circuit ends at the corner of the stone. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ has gone around the House, and the crowd is still turning. Jabir ibn Abdullah, who told the story of that pilgrimage in a report kept in Sahih Muslim, says what came next. The Prophet stepped out of the circle and walked a short way to a spot near the Ka'ba, reciting a line from the Qur'an as he went. Then he stood, with that spot between him and the House, and prayed. Today, the place he stopped.
screen: `THE SEVENTH CIRCUIT ENDS.` → `HE STEPS OUT OF THE CIRCLE.` → `HE STANDS, AND PRAYS.`

segments.voice: First, the verse he recited. It's in surah two, and Pickthall's translation reads: "Take as your place of worship the place where Abraham stood (to pray)." The Arabic name is maqam Ibrahim, the station of Ibrahim. Tradition says it's a stone Ibrahim stood on while he and his son built the House; today it sits in a small enclosure near the Ka'ba. Second, what the Prophet did there. Jabir says he placed the station between himself and the House and prayed two rak'ahs, two units of prayer. Jabir also reports what he recited in them: two short surahs, the one that begins Say: He is Allah, One, and the one that begins Say: O disbelievers. Abdullah ibn Umar, in Sahih al-Bukhari, gives the same order: the circuits, then two rak'ahs behind the station, then on to the next rite. Third, the posture of the place. After the moving, the crowd, the circling, the reaching for the stone, the pilgrim stops where Ibrahim is said to have stood, and prays toward the same House. The circle turns into a line, one person facing one direction. Fourth, look back, because this is where the week lands. The boundary. The two white cloths. The restraint they stand for. Here I am, said out loud for miles. Seven circuits around the center. A kiss, a touch, or a raised hand at the corner. And now two quiet rak'ahs at the place of the man who, in the Qur'an, built the House and called the people to it. Each piece this week has been one step. This one is the pause between them.
screen: `TAKE AS YOUR PLACE OF WORSHIP.` · `TWO RAK'AHS BEHIND THE STATION.` · `THE CIRCLE TURNS INTO A LINE.` · `A WEEK OF STEPS, THEN A PAUSE.`

segments.voice: If you're Muslim and pray, pray two rak'ahs now, and if you know them, recite the two short surahs the Prophet chose. If you don't pray, stand still for a minute facing one direction, any direction, on purpose, feet steady and hands at rest, and let the week's movement settle into one place.
Behind Ibrahim's station. The spot near the Ka'ba where pilgrims pray two rak'ahs after tawaf, following the verse and the Prophet's example. Today's word.
Your line: where ibrahim stood. After all the circling, one person, still, facing one way. Rest well.
